terms: Cohen subcultural theory
Albert Cohen (1955): status frustration leads working-class boys to invert middle-class values in delinquent subculture.
Durkheim on crime
Crime is inevitable and functional: boundary maintenance, adaptation, social change; anomie when norms break down.
Labelling theory
Becker (1963): deviance is created by social reaction; master status; deviant career; primary and secondary deviance.
Marxist crime
Chambliss (1975): criminal law protects bourgeois property; corporate crime largely ignored by enforcement.
Merton strain theory
1938: gap between cultural goals and legitimate means produces five responses, including innovation (crime).
Right realism
Wilson and Kelling (1982) Broken Windows: visible disorder invites further crime; rational choice underlies offending.
Feminism
Liberal (Friedan 1963), Marxist (Mitchell 1971), Radical (Firestone 1970), Black (hooks 1981) tackle patriarchy from different angles.
Modernity
Giddens (1990): high-modern society characterised by reflexivity, abstract systems and globalisation.
Postmodernity
Lyotard (1979): incredulity towards meta-narratives; identity fragmented and consumer-based.
Social action theory
Weber and symbolic interactionism (Mead 1934): meanings and interactions produce social reality; micro-level focus.
Structural theory
Functionalism and Marxism: society shapes individuals; macro-level analysis of institutions and norms.
Value freedom
Weber: sociology should separate facts from values in research, though value-relevance is unavoidable in question selection.
Demographic change
ONS (2022): UK fertility rate 1.49; mean age at first birth 30.9; cohabiting couple families fastest growing.
Family diversity
Rapoport and Rapoport (1982): organisational, cultural, class, life-course and cohort diversity reshape family forms.
Feminist family
Delphy and Leonard (1992): family is patriarchal; women's unpaid work benefits men more than the system.
Functionalist family
Parsons (1955): nuclear family performs primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personalities.
Marxist family
Zaretsky (1976): family reproduces capitalism by providing free domestic labour and a refuge for alienated workers.
Postmodern family
Stacey (1990): family is diverse and chosen; rise of divorce-extended, lone-parent and same-sex families.
Dependency theory
Frank (1967): development of the West caused underdevelopment of the South; metropolis-satellite chains of exploitation.
Human Development Index
UNDP composite of life expectancy, education and GNI per capita; UK scored 0.929 in 2022, Niger 0.394.
Modernisation theory
Rostow (1960) five stages: traditional, preconditions, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption.
Neoliberalism
Washington Consensus: free trade, deregulation, privatisation; criticised for widening inequality (Stiglitz 2002).
Sustainable Development Goals
UN 2015: 17 goals targeting 2030 - poverty, hunger, gender, climate; successor to Millennium Development Goals.
World systems
Wallerstein (1974): global economy divided into core, semi-periphery and periphery in unequal exchange.
Biomedical model
The dominant Western view that health is the absence of biological disease, treated by medical experts focusing on the body rather than social causes.
Health inequalities
Systematic differences in health and life expectancy between social groups by class, gender or ethnicity, often linked to material conditions.
Medicalisation
The process by which everyday or social conditions, such as sadness or childbirth, come to be defined and treated as medical problems.
Sick role
Talcott Parsons' idea that being ill is a temporary social role with rights (exemption from normal duties) and obligations (to seek help and try to recover).
Social construction of illness
The idea that what counts as 'illness' varies between cultures and over time, so definitions of health are shaped by society rather than fixed.
Social model of health
The view that health and illness are shaped by social factors such as poverty, environment and lifestyle, not by biology alone.
Digital divide
Inequality in access and skills; Ofcom (2023) found 6% of UK adults are 'narrow users' lacking digital skills.
Glasgow Media Group
Bad News (1976) found systematic bias in TV news framing; selection and presentation favoured establishment views.
Hypodermic model
Direct effects model; criticised for assuming passive audience; supported by Bandura's Bobo doll work.
Postmodern media
Baudrillard (1981): hyperreality - media simulations replace reality; Gulf War 'did not take place' as media event.
Reception theory
Hall (1980): audiences make dominant, negotiated or oppositional readings of media texts.
Uses and gratifications
Blumler and Katz (1974): audiences actively use media for diversion, identity, relationships and surveillance.
Absolute poverty
Rowntree (1901): inability to afford basic subsistence; World Bank uses $2.15 per day (2022).
Culture of poverty
Lewis (1959): poor develop fatalism and present-time orientation passed across generations; criticised for victim blaming.
Relative poverty
Townsend (1979): inability to participate in society's customary activities; UK uses 60% of median income.
Structural poverty
Westergaard and Resler (1976): poverty results from labour market and class structure, not behaviour.
Universal Credit
2013 UK reform merging six benefits; aimed at simplifying welfare and incentivising work; criticised for delays and conditionality.
Welfare state
Beveridge Report (1942) identified five giants - want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness; basis of post-war welfare.
Bourdieu (1977)
Cultural and educational capital; middle-class habitus matches school expectations, giving advantage.
Bowles and Gintis (1976)
Correspondence principle: schools mirror workplace hierarchy; hidden curriculum produces docile workers.
Durkheim on education
1893: schools transmit moral codes and shared values, creating social solidarity and preparing for division of labour.
Marketisation
1988 Education Reform Act introduced league tables, parental choice and competition; Ball (1994) 'parentocracy'.
Parsons on education
School is a focal socialising agency bridging family particularism and society's universalism; meritocratic role allocation.
Willis (1977)
Learning to Labour: 12 working-class 'lads' rejected school culture but their counter-culture ironically prepared them for manual work.
Cultural homogenisation
The idea that globalisation spreads a similar consumer culture worldwide, sometimes called Westernisation or McDonaldisation, reducing local diversity.
Digital divide
The gap between those with effective access to digital technology and the internet and those without, often along class, age or global lines.
Global village
McLuhan's term for a world drawn together by electronic media, where information spreads instantly and people share a common media culture.
Globalisation
The increasing interconnection of societies through trade, technology, media and migration, so events and cultures across the world influence one another.
Networked society
Castells' idea that social and economic life is increasingly organised around digital information networks rather than fixed physical places.
Time-space compression
Harvey's idea that modern communication and transport make distant places feel closer, allowing near-instant global connection and exchange.

religion-belief-faith-in-contemporary-so.d: Religion, Belief & Faith in Contemporary Society
terms: Liberation theology
Latin American Catholic movement (1960s): combined Marxism with Christianity to challenge poverty and dictatorship.
New religious movements
Wallis (1984): world-affirming, world-rejecting, world-accommodating sects classified by relation to society.
Religion and gender
Armstrong (1993): early religions worshipped goddesses; patriarchal monotheism marginalised women.
Religion as change
Weber: Calvinist Protestantism unintentionally produced capitalism, showing religion can drive change.
Religion as conservative
Durkheim: religion reinforces social cohesion and the status quo via collective rituals.
Secularisation
Bruce (2002): UK Christian affiliation fell from 72% in 2001 to 46% in 2021 (ONS Census).
Functionalism on inequality
Davis and Moore (1945): inequality is necessary to motivate the most talented to fill the most important positions.
Goldthorpe scheme
1980 Nuffield study: seven-class scheme based on employment relations; basis of NS-SEC used by ONS.
Marx on class
Two-class model: bourgeoisie own means of production, proletariat sell labour; objective class position drives conflict.
Underclass
Murray (1990): welfare-dependent group with deviant values; criticised for blaming victims of structural disadvantage.
Weber on class
Class (market position), status (prestige) and party (power) are three dimensions of stratification.
Wright (1985)
Neo-Marxist: contradictory class locations (managers) hold authority but sell labour; expands Marx's binary.
Globalisation
Increased worldwide interconnection through trade, media and migration; produces hybrid identities (Hall 1992).
Goffman's dramaturgy
Goffman (1959): social life is theatre; we present a 'front-stage' self while managing 'back-stage' identities.
Hyperreality
Baudrillard (1981): media simulations become more real than reality; identity formed by consumed signs.
Identity
Sense of self constructed through interaction with others; both personal (individual) and social (group) dimensions.
Postmodern identity
Bauman (2000) 'liquid modernity': identity is fluid, fragmented and self-chosen through consumption.
Socialisation
Process of learning culture; primary in family, secondary through school, media, peers, religion and work.
